newsitem.title: USA: Simpson civil trial brings scaled-down media sideshow.
newsitem.headline: Simpson civil trial brings scaled-down media sideshow.

text.p: With television coverage blacked out and attorneys muzzled by a "gag order" during O.J. Simpson's civil trial, "Camp O.J." -- where the international media was based for last year's criminal trial -- may never be the same.

Gone on Tuesday were the helicopters that seemed to perpetually circle the Criminal Courts building in downtown Los Angeles, hamstrung by a Santa Monica Superior Court order that prohibited filming or videotaping certain areas of the building for security reasons.
Gone were profiteers, who set up shop on the sidewalks outside the building to sell buttons, hats, T-shirts and other Simpson paraphernalia, banned by a Santa Monica city ordinance.
And largely absent were publicity seekers, activists and the simply curious who turned out in large numbers for the start of the first trial, perhaps finally burned out on the Simpson spectacle.
But the "circus atmosphere" that Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki worked so hard to prevent was not entirely absent.

Early on Tuesday morning, hours before lawyers were scheduled to arrive for the first court session, the lawn in front of the courthouse was teeming with reporters, the street jammed with television trucks.
Expert legal commentators, many of them recognisable from similar roles at last year's criminal trial, spoke into cameras as they forecast the courtroom skirmishes ahead.

A few token eccentrics also showed up, waving placards in support of one side or another. They included criminal case regulars Larry "Melrose" Green -- still calling for Simpson to "fry" even though he was no longer on trial for his life.

Larry Mays was back, carrying his banner and loudly advising anyone who will listen to "Ask Jesus to Save You." Mays, who paced in front of the Los Angeles courts building nearly every day during the first trial, promises that he will be around for the duration of the civil case as well.
For the most part, the scene reflected a much mellower, smaller version of the criminal trial. Even the press contingent has been reduced and kept better corralled.

At the criminal trial reporters occupied an entire floor of the Criminal Courts building, with broadcast organisations also squatting in "Camp O.J." -- a car park full of caravans. Reporters sat on scaffolding high above the throng to deliver daily reports.

At the civil trial, the print press has been banished across the street to a small hotel conference room while television crews have set up "Camp O.J. By-the-Sea," 14 trailers on the lot of the Rand Corp. think tank.
Ron Olsen, a veteran reporter for local TV station KTLA, who also covered the criminal trial, surveyed the relatively quiet scene and mused that the civil trial "hasn't really been a circus yet.
"Wait until O.J. shows up to testify. Then we'll see a circus," he said.
